common.siteDescription: Learning algorithms and data structures for web developers

home.heroDescription: Understanding algorithms and data structures is a key skill for developers. We help you master them through clear animations and step-by-step visualizations.
home.searchDesc: Search algorithms help find elements in data structures quickly and efficiently.
home.sortingDesc: Sorting algorithms arrange data in order — a fundamental skill in programming.

binary-search.title: Binary Search
binary-search.description: Binary search is an algorithm for finding an element in a sorted array by repeatedly dividing the search interval in half. At each step, the algorithm compares the middle element of the array with the target value and eliminates the half where the element cannot exist.
binary-search.whyItMatters: Binary search is a fundamental algorithm constantly used in web development: searching sorted data, autocomplete, database index lookups, implementing bisect functions. Understanding binary search helps you grasp how database indexes work and why they're so fast.

howItWorks.title: How the Algorithm Works
howItWorks.intro: Binary search is based on the divide-and-conquer principle. Instead of checking each element one by one (like linear search), the algorithm cuts the search space in half with every step.
howItWorks.step1: Set two pointers: left (start of the array) and right (end of the array). These pointers define the current range where we're searching for the target element.
howItWorks.step2: Calculate the middle index: mid = left + (right - left) / 2. Using this formula instead of (left + right) / 2 prevents integer overflow when working with large arrays.
howItWorks.step3: Compare arr[mid] with the target value. There are three possible outcomes:
howItWorks.step3a: arr[mid] == target — element found, return index mid.
howItWorks.step3b: arr[mid] < target — the target is in the right half. Set left = mid + 1.
howItWorks.step3c: arr[mid] > target — the target is in the left half. Set right = mid - 1.
howItWorks.step4: Repeat steps 2–3 while left ≤ right. If the pointers cross (left > right), the element is not in the array — return -1.
howItWorks.exampleStep1: Step 1: left=0, right=6, mid=3 → arr[3]=7 == 7. Found in 1 step!
howItWorks.exampleStep2: For comparison: with linear search in an array of 1,000,000 elements, binary search finds the element in at most 20 steps (log₂ 1,000,000 ≈ 20).

complexityAnalysis.title: Complexity Analysis
complexityAnalysis.timeBest: O(1) — best case, when the target element happens to be exactly in the middle of the array on the first step.
complexityAnalysis.timeAverage: O(log n) — average case. At each step, the algorithm discards half of the remaining elements. For an array of n elements, it takes at most ⌈log₂ n⌉ comparisons.
complexityAnalysis.timeWorst: O(log n) — worst case. The element is at the edge of the array or not present at all, but even then the number of steps depends logarithmically on the array size.
complexityAnalysis.spaceIterative: O(1) — iterative implementation uses only a few variables (left, right, mid) that don't depend on the input size.
complexityAnalysis.spaceRecursive: O(log n) — recursive implementation uses a call stack of depth log₂ n.
complexityAnalysis.comparison: Linear search has O(n) complexity — in the worst case it checks all n elements. Binary search reduces this to O(log n). For an array of 1 billion elements: linear search — up to 1,000,000,000 steps, binary search — up to 30 steps.

applications.title: Real-World Applications
applications.app1: Any sorted dataset is a perfect candidate for binary search. Dictionaries, phone books, reference tables — they all use the principle of halving the search space.
applications.app2: B-trees, which underpin indexes in PostgreSQL, MySQL, and other DBMS, use binary search at each level of the tree to quickly find the right page. This is why indexed lookups by ID work in milliseconds even on tables with billions of rows.
applications.app3: The bisect module in Python's standard library implements binary search for inserting elements into a sorted list while maintaining order. Used for priority queues, running medians, and window functions.
applications.app4: When typing in a search box, the system finds the lower and upper bounds of matching suggestions using binary search on a sorted dictionary.
applications.app5: Binary search is used to find the first element ≥ target (lower_bound) and the first element > target (upper_bound). This is the foundation for implementing sets and range queries in C++ STL.
applications.app6: A paradoxical application: when a direct solution is hard, but you can check whether a candidate answer is "good enough." Used in optimization problems: minimum time, maximum distance, minimum weight — if the answer can be verified in polynomial time.

steps.goRight: arr[{mid}] = {value} < {target}, excluding left half, searching right
steps.goLeft: arr[{mid}] = {value} > {target}, excluding right half, searching left

bubble-sort.title: Bubble Sort
bubble-sort.description: Bubble sort is a simple sorting algorithm that repeatedly walks through the array, compares adjacent elements, and swaps them if they are in the wrong order. The process repeats until the array is fully sorted.
bubble-sort.whyItMatters: While bubble sort is rarely used in production due to its inefficiency, it's an excellent learning algorithm for understanding sorting principles, element comparison, and value swapping. It's the foundation for understanding more complex sorting algorithms.

howItWorks.title: How the Algorithm Works
howItWorks.intro: Bubble sort gets its name from the way larger elements gradually "bubble up" to the end of the array, like air bubbles rising in water. The algorithm makes multiple passes through the array, swapping adjacent elements that are out of order.
howItWorks.step1: Begin at the first element of the array. We'll compare each pair of adjacent elements during a left-to-right pass.
howItWorks.step2: Compare the current element with the next one. If the current element is greater than the next, they are in the wrong order.
howItWorks.step3: If the elements are out of order, swap them. There are two possible outcomes:
howItWorks.step3a: arr[j] > arr[j+1] — swap the elements, the larger one moves right.
howItWorks.step3b: arr[j] ≤ arr[j+1] — no swap needed, move to the next pair.
howItWorks.step4: After one complete pass, the largest unsorted element is guaranteed to be at the end. Repeat passes for the remaining unsorted portion until no swaps are needed — the array is sorted.

complexityAnalysis.title: Complexity Analysis
complexityAnalysis.timeBest: O(n) — best case occurs when the array is already sorted. With the optimization (checking if any swaps occurred), the algorithm makes only one pass and terminates early.
complexityAnalysis.timeAverage: O(n²) — average case. For a randomly ordered array, the algorithm makes approximately n²/2 comparisons and n²/4 swaps on average.
complexityAnalysis.timeWorst: O(n²) — worst case, when the array is sorted in reverse order. Every pair of adjacent elements needs to be swapped on every pass, resulting in n·(n-1)/2 comparisons.
complexityAnalysis.spaceInPlace: O(1) — bubble sort is an in-place algorithm. It only uses a constant amount of additional memory for temporary variables during swapping (and the swapped flag for optimization).
complexityAnalysis.spaceStable: Stable sort — equal elements never change their relative order because swaps only happen when arr[j] > arr[j+1] (strictly greater), not when equal.
complexityAnalysis.optimization: The key optimization is tracking whether any swaps occurred during a pass. If a complete pass finishes without any swaps, the array is already sorted and the algorithm can stop immediately. This improves best-case performance from O(n²) to O(n).

applications.title: Real-World Applications
applications.app1: Bubble sort is the most intuitive sorting algorithm for beginners. It clearly demonstrates the core concepts: comparing elements, swapping values, and repeating until sorted. Most computer science courses start with bubble sort.
applications.app2: When data is already nearly sorted (only a few elements out of place), bubble sort with early termination can be quite efficient — it finishes in O(n) time with just one or two passes.
applications.app3: For very small arrays (5–10 elements), bubble sort's simplicity can make it competitive with more complex algorithms due to low overhead and good cache locality.
applications.app4Title: Checking if an Array Is Sorted
applications.app4: A single pass of bubble sort (without swaps) is essentially an O(n) check for whether an array is already sorted — useful as a pre-check before running a more expensive algorithm.
applications.app5: In computer graphics, bubble sort is sometimes used for small lists in polygon filling algorithms and depth sorting, where the number of elements is tiny and simplicity matters more than asymptotic performance.

steps.passComplete: Pass {pass} complete. Largest element has 'bubbled up' to the end.

insertion-sort.title: Insertion Sort
insertion-sort.description: Insertion sort is a simple sorting algorithm that builds the final sorted array one element at a time. It works similarly to how you sort playing cards in your hands — you take one card at a time and insert it into the correct position among the already sorted cards.
insertion-sort.whyItMatters: Insertion sort is one of the simplest sorting algorithms, yet it has important practical applications. It's efficient for small datasets and nearly-sorted data. Understanding insertion sort teaches you the concept of incremental sorting and adaptive algorithms.

howItWorks.title: How the Algorithm Works
howItWorks.intro: Insertion sort builds a sorted array one element at a time. It takes each element from the unsorted portion and inserts it into its correct position in the sorted portion, shifting larger elements as needed.
howItWorks.step1: The first element is considered sorted by itself. The rest of the array is unsorted.
howItWorks.step2: Take the first unsorted element — this is your 'key'. Compare it with elements in the sorted portion, moving from right to left.
howItWorks.step3: If the key is smaller than the compared element, shift that element one position to the right. Continue until you find the correct position for the key:
howItWorks.step3a: Shift: Move elements greater than the key one position to the right.
howItWorks.step3b: Insert: Place the key in its correct position in the sorted portion.
howItWorks.step4: Continue picking the next unsorted element and inserting it into the sorted portion. When all elements have been processed, the array is fully sorted.
howItWorks.exampleStep1: Pick 11, compare with 12 → 11 < 12, shift 12 right → insert 11 at position 0. Array: [11, 12, 13, 5, 6].
howItWorks.exampleStep2: Pick 13, compare with 12 → 13 > 12, stays. Pick 5, shift 13, 12, 11 → insert 5 at position 0. Array: [5, 11, 12, 13, 6].

complexityAnalysis.title: Complexity Analysis
complexityAnalysis.timeBest: O(n) — best case occurs when the array is already sorted. Each element is compared only once with its predecessor, resulting in a single pass through the array.
complexityAnalysis.timeAverage: O(n²) — on average, each element needs to be compared with about half of the sorted portion. This results in roughly n²/4 comparisons.
complexityAnalysis.timeWorst: O(n²) — worst case occurs when the array is sorted in reverse order. Each new element must be compared with all elements in the sorted portion and shifted to the beginning.
complexityAnalysis.spaceInPlace: O(1) — insertion sort works in-place, requiring only a single extra variable to store the key element. No additional arrays are needed.
complexityAnalysis.spaceStable: Stable — equal elements maintain their relative order. This is because we only shift elements greater than the key, not equal to it.
complexityAnalysis.adaptive: Insertion sort is adaptive — it performs better on partially sorted data. If the array is nearly sorted, the algorithm approaches O(n) time complexity. This makes it useful as the final phase of more complex algorithms like Shell sort or Timsort.

applications.title: Real-World Applications
applications.app1: Insertion sort is often used for small datasets (n < 50) where its simplicity and low overhead make it faster than more complex algorithms. Many hybrid algorithms switch to insertion sort for small subarrays.
applications.app2: Insertion sort can sort data as it arrives (online algorithm). Each new element is inserted into the correct position in the already-sorted portion, making it ideal for streaming data.
applications.app3: Timsort, the default sorting algorithm in Python and Java, uses insertion sort for small runs (typically ≤ 32 elements). It exploits the fact that insertion sort is very efficient for small, partially sorted data.
applications.app4: When data is already mostly sorted (e.g., adding a few new records to a sorted database), insertion sort runs in nearly linear time, making it the optimal choice.
applications.app5: Insertion sort is often the first sorting algorithm taught because of its intuitive logic (sorting cards) and simple implementation. It helps students understand the concept of incremental algorithms.

merge-sort.title: Merge Sort
merge-sort.description: Merge sort is an efficient, stable sorting algorithm that uses a divide-and-conquer strategy. It recursively splits the array into two halves, sorts each half, and then merges the sorted halves back together. The merge step is the key operation: it combines two sorted sub-arrays into one sorted array.
merge-sort.whyItMatters: Merge sort guarantees O(n log n) time complexity in all cases, making it reliable for large datasets. It's the foundation for many external sorting algorithms used in databases and file systems. Understanding merge sort teaches you the divide-and-conquer paradigm and the concept of merging sorted sequences — a pattern used in merge joins, stream processing, and version control systems.

howItWorks.title: How the Algorithm Works
howItWorks.intro: Merge sort is a classic divide-and-conquer algorithm. It works by recursively splitting the array into smaller sub-arrays until each contains a single element, then merging them back together in sorted order.
howItWorks.step1: Split the array into two halves at the midpoint. If the array has 1 or 0 elements, it's already sorted — this is the base case for recursion.
howItWorks.step2: Apply merge sort recursively to the left half and the right half. Each recursive call splits further until reaching sub-arrays of size 1.
howItWorks.step3: Combine two sorted sub-arrays into one sorted array using a two-pointer technique:
howItWorks.step3a: Compare the first elements of each half. Take the smaller one and advance that pointer.
howItWorks.step3b: When one half is exhausted, copy all remaining elements from the other half.
howItWorks.step4: The merged array is now fully sorted. Return it up the recursion chain. After all merges complete, the entire array is sorted.
howItWorks.exampleStep2: Merge: [27, 38] and [3, 43] → compare 27 vs 3 → take 3 → compare 27 vs 43 → take 27 → ... → [3, 27, 38, 43].

complexityAnalysis.title: Complexity Analysis
complexityAnalysis.timeBest: O(n log n) — even in the best case, merge sort still performs all the split and merge operations. The number of levels is log₂ n, and each level does O(n) work for merging.
complexityAnalysis.timeAverage: O(n log n) — the average case is the same as best and worst. Merge sort's performance is deterministic and doesn't depend on the input data distribution.
complexityAnalysis.timeWorst: O(n log n) — unlike quick sort, merge sort has no degenerate case. It always divides the array evenly and merges in linear time at each level.
complexityAnalysis.spaceAuxiliary: O(n) — merge sort requires additional temporary arrays for the merge step. At each level of recursion, auxiliary arrays of total size n are created.
complexityAnalysis.spaceStable: Stable sort — equal elements maintain their relative order because during merging, when elements are equal, the left half's element is taken first (left[i] <= right[j]).
complexityAnalysis.comparison: Quick sort has O(n log n) average time but O(n²) worst case, while merge sort guarantees O(n log n) in all cases. However, merge sort uses O(n) extra memory, whereas quick sort works in-place with O(log n) stack space. In practice, quick sort is often faster due to better cache locality.

applications.title: Real-World Applications
applications.app1: When data doesn't fit in memory, databases use external merge sort: sorted runs are written to disk and then merged in passes. This is how PostgreSQL and other DBMS sort large datasets during ORDER BY and CREATE INDEX operations.
applications.app2: Many languages use merge sort (or its variant, Timsort) as the stable sorting algorithm. Python's sorted(), Java's Collections.sort() for objects, and Rust's stable sort all rely on merge sort under the hood.
applications.app3: The merge join algorithm in SQL databases works like the merge step of merge sort: two sorted streams are combined in a single pass. This is one of the most efficient join strategies when both inputs are already sorted.
applications.app4: A classic problem: count how many pairs (i, j) exist where i < j but arr[i] > arr[j]. Merge sort can be modified to count inversions during the merge step in O(n log n) time — used in recommendation systems and measuring data similarity.
applications.app5: When merging multiple sorted event streams (logs, time-series data, Kafka topics), the merge step of merge sort is used directly. This pattern appears in distributed systems, log aggregation, and time-series databases.
applications.app6: Git and other version control systems use merge algorithms based on the longest common subsequence and merge sort principles to combine changes from different branches into a single result.

quick-sort.title: Quick Sort
quick-sort.description: Quick sort is an efficient sorting algorithm that uses a divide-and-conquer strategy. It selects a pivot element and partitions the array into two sub-arrays: elements less than or equal to the pivot, and elements greater than the pivot. The sub-arrays are then sorted recursively.
quick-sort.whyItMatters: Quick sort is one of the most widely used sorting algorithms in practice. It's the default sorting algorithm in many programming languages and standard libraries. Understanding quick sort teaches you the divide-and-conquer paradigm, which is fundamental to many efficient algorithms.

howItWorks.title: How the Algorithm Works
howItWorks.intro: Quick sort uses the divide-and-conquer strategy: it picks a pivot element, partitions the array around it so that smaller elements go left and larger elements go right, then recursively sorts both sides.
howItWorks.step1: Select an element from the array to use as the pivot. Common strategies: last element, first element, random element, or median-of-three. The pivot choice affects performance but not correctness.
howItWorks.step2: Rearrange elements so that all values less than or equal to the pivot come before it, and all values greater come after it. After partitioning, the pivot is in its final sorted position.
howItWorks.step3: Apply quick sort to the left sub-array (elements before pivot) and the right sub-array (elements after pivot):
howItWorks.step3a: Left sub-array: all elements ≤ pivot — sort recursively.
howItWorks.step3b: Right sub-array: all elements > pivot — sort recursively.
howItWorks.step4: When a sub-array has 0 or 1 elements, it's already sorted — stop recursion. After all recursive calls complete, the entire array is sorted.
howItWorks.exampleStep1: Partition: [10, 30, 40, 50] < 70 < [80, 90]. Pivot 70 is now at index 4 (final position).
howItWorks.exampleStep2: Recurse left: [10, 30, 40, 50] → already partitioned. Recurse right: [80, 90] → 80 < 90, done. Result: [10, 30, 40, 50, 70, 80, 90].

complexityAnalysis.title: Complexity Analysis
complexityAnalysis.timeBest: O(n log n) — best case occurs when the pivot always divides the array into two roughly equal halves. This gives log₂ n levels of recursion, each doing O(n) work for partitioning.
complexityAnalysis.timeAverage: O(n log n) — on average, quick sort performs very well. Random pivot selection makes the expected depth of recursion O(log n), giving O(n log n) total work.
complexityAnalysis.timeWorst: O(n²) — worst case occurs when the pivot is always the smallest or largest element (e.g., already sorted array with last-element pivot). This creates n levels of recursion with O(n) work each.
complexityAnalysis.spaceInPlace: O(log n) — quick sort works in-place (no extra arrays), but the recursion stack uses O(log n) space on average. In the worst case, the stack can grow to O(n).
complexityAnalysis.spaceNotStable: Not stable — equal elements may change their relative order during partitioning. If stability is required, merge sort is preferred.
complexityAnalysis.pivotStrategy: The choice of pivot critically affects performance. Last/first element — simple but O(n²) on sorted data. Random element — good expected performance. Median-of-three — examines first, middle, last and picks the median, providing good practical performance. Introselect (used in std::sort) — switches to heap sort if recursion depth exceeds 2·log(n).

applications.title: Real-World Applications
applications.app1: Many programming languages use quick sort (or its hybrid variants) as the default sorting algorithm. C's qsort(), C++'s std::sort (introsort — quick sort + heap sort), and Java's Arrays.sort() for primitive types all rely on quick sort.
applications.app2: Databases use quick sort for in-memory sorting of query results. When the optimizer chooses a sort-based plan, quick sort's cache efficiency makes it faster than merge sort for data that fits in RAM.
applications.app3: Quick select — a variant of quick sort — finds the kth smallest element in O(n) average time. Used for finding medians, percentiles, and top-K elements without fully sorting the data.
applications.app4: Quick sort and its variants are used in computational geometry (e.g., sorting points for convex hull), signal processing, and numerical analysis where in-place sorting with good cache performance is critical.
applications.app5: The partition step of quick sort is a standalone useful operation: separating passing/failing students, dividing data into above/below threshold groups, or implementing the Dutch National Flag problem (Sort Colors on LeetCode).
